content.text: An MCP server can expose three kinds of things, and each has a different decider. Tools are model-controlled: Claude chooses when to call them. Resources are application-controlled: the host decides which data becomes context. Prompts are user-controlled: a person picks them, often as a slash command. Exposing everything as a tool hands every decision to the model, including the ones that belong to your users.

items.text: Tutorials usually start with a tool or two, and many never get further.
Tool calls are the visible part: you watch Claude call a tool and read the result in the transcript.
Some integrations really are tools-only. Of the MCP feature set, the Claude API's MCP connector says "only tool calls are currently supported."
The protocol's name puts the model first, so it's natural to assume the model drives every part of it.

content.text: The half-truth: tools are model-controlled. But MCP defines three server primitives, and two of them are deliberately kept out of the model's hands.
The docs summarize the server side in one table, with a column for who controls each primitive:

rows.text: Claude calls them; you approve or deny

content.text: The useful question when you design a server isn't "what can it do?" but "who should decide when this happens?" Get it wrong one way and the model pulls in context nobody asked for, or skips a workflow a person wanted to start. Get it wrong the other way and people have to trigger, by hand, actions the model could have handled on its own.
Tools: the model decides, a human can say no

The docs call tools model-controlled, "meaning AI models can discover and invoke them automatically." They pair that with human oversight: hosts can show which tools are available, ask for approval before individual calls and keep a log of every execution. Tools fit actions and live queries: restarting a worker, searching tickets, creating a calendar event.

The docs add that "prompt results are injected directly into the conversation", so the review format comes from your server every time instead of from Claude's improvisation. The flip side is trust: the server writes that text, so running a prompt is like pasting the server's words into your chat. Give prompt-bearing servers the same scrutiny as any code you install.

How to apply it in your project
For each thing your server offers, ask who should trigger it: the model, the application or a person. Only the first group should be tools.
Schemas, runbooks, configs and docs get stable URIs. Use resource templates for families of records, such as
Reviews, reports and checklists that a person starts on purpose become prompts with a few clear arguments.

items.title: Keep tools for actions and live queries

content.text: Give them precise descriptions and let the host's approval flow guard anything with side effects.

items.text: MCP servers expose tools, resources and prompts, not just tools.
Tools are model-controlled, resources application-controlled, and prompts user-controlled.
Resources are URI-addressed context the host decides to load; Claude Code attaches them with
